Chapter 9: Putting Multiplying into Practice—Everyday Tools and Habits.
So, becoming a Multiplier isn’t just a one-and-done thing. It’s really about building new habits, trying out fresh approaches, and always reflecting on how your leadership is landing with others.
Want to know how to put those Multiplier disciplines into action in real life? Here are some simple, practical tools you can start using right away.
First, start small. Pick just one discipline to focus on for a week. Maybe you choose to be a Debate Maker—so you invite more input during meetings. Or, you might flex your Investor muscle by delegating a meaningful task, then stepping back and letting someone run with it. It’s all about experimenting and seeing what works best for you and your team.
Next, try swapping out instructions for powerful questions. Instead of telling people what to do, ask “why?” or “what if?” These kinds of questions really get people thinking and open up new possibilities.
Another helpful habit? Make yourself a “stop doing” list. Take a moment to notice any behaviors that might be holding your team back—things like interrupting, micromanaging, or always needing to have the last word. Just being aware of these habits can help you dial them down.
And remember, it’s not only about hitting big results. Celebrate learning, too. When people take risks, learn from mistakes, or pick up new skills—even when things don’t go perfectly—recognize it. That kind of encouragement goes a long way.
Feedback is your friend. Make it a habit to check in with your team regularly. Ask what’s working, and what could be better in your leadership approach. This keeps everyone growing together.
One more thing—don’t be afraid to show a little vulnerability. Share your own learning journey, your mistakes, and what you’re trying to improve. When you’re open like this, it creates a safe space for everyone else to do the same.
Picture this: a team leader kicks off each week by asking, “What’s one thing I can do to help you grow this week?” It’s such a simple question, but over time, it totally shifts the team’s culture toward ownership and development.
And here’s something to keep in mind—multiplying isn’t a solo act. It’s a team sport. Encourage others to try out these Multiplier habits, too, and look for ways to support each other. When everyone’s committed to multiplying intelligence, the whole team rises together.
